tagline: Art nouveau and amber on the Baltic
overview:
Latvia is the middle of the three Baltic states, lying between Estonia and Lithuania on the eastern shore of the Baltic Sea, with Russia and Belarus to the east. It is about the size of West Virginia, flat and green, with about half of the land covered in forest. The capital, Riga, sits where the Daugava River meets the sea and is the largest city in the Baltic states. Its old town of church spires and its avenues of ornate art nouveau buildings, decorated with faces, flowers, and mythical beasts, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Around 1.9 million people live in Latvia, and the population has shrunk as many have moved to Western Europe for work. Latvian, one of only two surviving Baltic languages, is the official tongue, and Russian is spoken by a large minority. Latvia is a parliamentary republic that regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991 and joined the European Union and NATO in 2004. Its people are known for choral singing, midsummer celebrations, and a deep bond with forests, rivers, and the sea.
landAndNature: Latvia is low and gently rolling, with the highest hill, Gaiziņkalns, reaching only 312 meters. Nearly 500 kilometers of coastline face the Baltic Sea and the Gulf of Riga, with long white sand beaches backed by pine forests, and amber washes ashore after storms. The Daugava is the great river, and the Gauja winds through a valley of sandstone cliffs and caves in Gauja National Park. Thousands of lakes and vast bogs dot the east, and Kemeri National Park has raised bogs crossed by boardwalks. Forests of pine, spruce, and birch cover half the country and hide wolves, lynx, brown bears, and huge numbers of beavers, deer, and wild boar. White storks nest in almost every village, and the Ventas Rumba on the Venta River is the widest waterfall in Europe.
peopleAndCulture: Latvians celebrate the summer solstice, Jāņi, more than almost any other holiday: people wear oak-leaf and flower crowns, eat caraway cheese, sing, and stay up all night around bonfires. Every five years the Song and Dance Celebration gathers tens of thousands of singers and dancers in Riga. Traditional food includes gray peas with bacon, rye bread, smoked fish, and cold beet soup in summer. Most Latvians are Lutheran, Catholic, or Orthodox. Ice hockey is the national sport, and Latvia has won medals in basketball, bobsled, and luge; the country also produced the world's top 3x3 basketball team. Folk songs called dainas, more than a million lines of them, are a national treasure, and the Riga Central Market fills five old zeppelin hangars.
history: Baltic tribes such as the Latgalians, Livonians, and Curonians lived here for thousands of years before German crusaders conquered the region in the 1200s and founded Riga in 1201. German nobles and merchants ruled for centuries under Polish, Swedish, and, from the 1700s, Russian control. Latvian national feeling grew in the 1800s, and Latvia declared independence in 1918 as the Russian Empire collapsed. The Soviet Union occupied the country in 1940, followed by Nazi Germany, during which most of Latvia's Jews were murdered, and then Soviet rule again from 1944, with tens of thousands deported to Siberia. In 1989 Latvians joined the Baltic Way human chain, and independence was restored in 1991. Latvia joined the EU and NATO in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2014.
funFacts: Riga has about 800 art nouveau buildings, more than any other city in the world.
Latvia's Ventas Rumba waterfall is only about two meters high but nearly 250 meters wide, the widest in Europe.
Riga's Christmas market claims the first decorated public Christmas tree, set up in 1510.
Latvians have collected more than 1.2 million folk song texts, so many that the collection is kept in a special cabinet.
About 200,000 Latvians, a tenth of the population, formed a human chain across the Baltics in 1989 to demand freedom.
